title: Narrative Essays: Telling a Story That Holds the Reader

blocks.text: Two candidates answer the same question: "Write a story about a day you will never forget." The first writes four hundred words about waking up, brushing his teeth, eating bread and tea, and boarding a bus. Nothing goes wrong. The second begins: "The bus had travelled only twenty minutes when the driver, without a word, pulled off the expressway and switched off the engine." Only one of them has written a story.

blocks.markdown:
A **narrative essay** recounts a sequence of events. It is not a description of a place and it is not a list of everything that happened in a day. What turns events into a story is a **problem** — something at stake that the reader wants to see settled.

That is why every good narrative, from a folktale told under a mango tree to a novel, follows the same underlying shape.

blocks.title: Narrative structure
blocks.text: **Orientation** — who, where and when. **Complication** — the problem that disturbs the situation. **Climax** — the moment of greatest tension, where the outcome is decided. **Resolution** — how things settle afterwards.

rows: Establishes place, time and the main character
Introduces the problem and lets it grow
blocks.caption: Proportion matters: candidates who spend half the essay setting the scene run out of room for the story

blocks.markdown:
### Hold one tense and one viewpoint

A narrative recounts what has already happened, so the **simple past** is your base tense: *walked*, *shouted*, *ran*. When you need to reach further back — a memory, a flashback — use the **past perfect**: *my father had warned me about that road*.

The **viewpoint** must also stay fixed. If the story opens with *I*, everything is seen through that character's eyes and stays that way to the last line. Switching from *I* to *he* for the same person confuses the reader and is marked down as an organisation fault.

### Show, do not tell

Compare these two sentences:

- *I was very afraid as I entered the dark corridor.*
- *My hand stayed on the door frame long after the light had gone, and I counted my own breathing.*

The first names the emotion. The second gives the reader the evidence and lets them feel it. **Showing** means choosing physical, specific detail: what was heard, seen, smelt or touched.

blocks.title: Planning a narrative in five minutes
blocks.prompt: Write a story that ends with the words: "...and that was the last time I ever took a shortcut."

steps.text: Read the rubric for anything fixed. Here the final sentence is given, so the story must genuinely arrive at it — a shortcut must be taken and must go wrong.
Decide the complication before anything else. A shortcut through an uncompleted building at dusk; the narrator gets trapped when the only gate is padlocked.
Fix the viewpoint and tense: first person, simple past. Write them at the top of your rough plan so you do not drift.

Sketch the four stages in single lines — orientation: leaving school late after extra lessons; complication: choosing the shortcut, hearing the gate close; climax: the torch battery dies while he is halfway up the stairwell; resolution: the night watchman's voice at dawn.
Choose three sensory details in advance and mark where each will go — the smell of wet cement, the sound of pigeons in the roof, the cold of the iron railing.
Write, keeping the orientation short. Aim to have the complication running by the end of the first paragraph.
Land the ending on the given sentence exactly as printed, with no extra moral added after it.

blocks.answer: A four-stage plan with viewpoint and tense fixed in advance, three sensory details placed, and the prescribed sentence used as the true final line.

blocks.markdown:
### Dialogue

A line or two of speech brings a story to life, but it must be punctuated correctly:

> "Where are the answer scripts?" the invigilator shouted.

> "Come down slowly," he said, "and hold the rail."

The spoken words sit inside quotation marks; the comma or question mark that ends them goes **inside** the closing mark; and the reporting phrase — *he said* — begins in lower case because it belongs to the same sentence. Start a new paragraph each time the speaker changes.

blocks.title: Endings examiners have read a thousand times
blocks.text: *And then I woke up and realised it was all a dream* cancels everything that happened, so the complication is never actually resolved. *That was the happiest day of my life* and *I thank God for saving me* are equally worn. Let the last event of the story do the work instead.

items: Begin inside the action, not with an announcement such as *In this essay I am going to narrate...*
Cut weak intensifiers — *very*, *so much*, *really* — and replace them with a specific detail.
Give the main character something to want, and something in the way of getting it.
Use the past perfect for anything that happened before the main action.
Vary sentence length: short sentences accelerate the climax.
Reread the last paragraph and ask whether the problem raised at the start has actually been settled.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: Marks are awarded for content, organisation, expression and mechanical accuracy. A story with a clear complication and resolution scores on content and organisation before the examiner has looked at a single verb. Spend the first five minutes planning those four stages — it is the cheapest way to gain marks in the whole paper.

points: A narrative runs orientation, complication, climax, resolution.
Keep the orientation short; the story lives in the complication and climax.
The base tense is the simple past, with the past perfect for earlier events.
The narrative viewpoint, once chosen, never changes.
Show emotion through physical detail rather than naming it.
Punctuate dialogue correctly and start a new paragraph for each speaker.
Avoid the dream ending and other clichés; let the events themselves close the story.
